To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have detected H-alpha emission in a sample of 6 star forming galaxies at a redshift of z~1.

we have demonstrated that it is possible to obtain high-quality spectra of galaxies at z~1 in a reasonable amount of time, and that the star formation rates derived from these spectra are consistent with those found in the rest-uv and rest-uv+IR.
We have demonstrated the feasibility of using multi-object near-in infrared spectroscopy on high-redshift galaxies to study star formation at z~1 using H-alpha.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What fraction of the star formation at z~1 is obscured?
- the star formation rate density of galaxies at z~1 - the evolution of the star formation rate function - the evolution of star formation in different galaxy populations.

- the true star formation activity of the universe at redshifts z~1, - the use of H-alpha to trace star formation at these redshifts, and - the development of new instrumentation to make this possible.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1) The H-alpha luminosity function is consistent with the predictions of the local H-alpha luminosity functions of Kennicutt et al (1983) and Hunter et al (1993) and with the UV luminosity function of Madau et al. (1998), but is inconsistent with the H-alpha luminosity of the local luminosity functions of Gallego et al. (2000), which are a factor of 2 lower than our results.
the CIRPASS system works well, and that we have obtained the first H-alpha spectra of galaxies at z~1.
(1) We have detected 5 H-alpha emitting galaxies at z~1 with CIRPASS, in a 15arcmin field.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the star formation activity of z~1 is not significantly different from the star formation activity at z~0, as suggested by some previous results, but rather is similar to the star formation activity in the local universe.
we have successfully demonstrated multi-object NIR spectroscopy, and that we have obtained H-alpha detections of galaxies at z~1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
star formation at this redshift is much more modest than previous estimates have suggested.
the star formation history at z~1 is not a simple extrapolation of the local star formation history, and that the peak of star activity is not at z~1.
the star formation rate density of the universe at redshift one is a factor of two to four higher than previous estimates.
